title: datasette-maplibre 0.1a0
text: Release: datasette-maplibre 0.1a0 The first new Datasette geospatial plugin in quite a while! This one combines the excellent MapLibre GL library with OpenFreeMap , the free vector map server operated by Zsolt Ero (you should sponsor Zsolt on GitHub .) I built most of this with a single prompt to Claude Fable 5.2: Look at datasette-cluster-map and datasette-leaflet-geojson plugins, then look at ~/dev/tools/openfreemap-demo.html - then build a brand new Datasette plugin that uses maplibreGL and openfreemap and combines the features of those other two plugins - but be creative and think outside the box for other useful features the plugin might have "Be creative and think outside the box" resulted in a few neat ideas - my favorite is that it displays SVG previews of GeoJSON shapes, then loads a WebGL preview only when they scroll into view. I also had Claude build a comprehensive demo which works in the latest Datasette Lite, so you can visit this link to load the plugin and a demo database in your browser via Pyodide and WebAssembly. I like this demo page showing both GeoJSON shapes and lat/lon points on the same map: Tags: visualization , generative-ai , datasette-lite , claude-mythos-fable , ai , llms , geospatial , openstreetmap , datasette

title: datasette-apps 0.4a0
text: Release: datasette-apps 0.4a0 Datasette Apps are sandboxed HTML and JavaScript applications that live inside Datasette - think Claude Artifacts, but these ones can run SQL queries against your data. 0.4a0 adds support for linking: you can link to an app with #fragments in the URL and the app can see and use those, plus supported URL schemes are reported back to Datasette Agent so it can help write apps that link to each other. This means you can have e.g. an app that shows details about a specific record, and a completely separate app that searches those records and links to their representations in the first app. Tags: datasette-agent , datasette-apps , datasette , urls

title: Ask HN: Stripe closed us after one $1,500 invoice and never asked for evidence
author: snirgbs
text: We're a small business that sells pre-booked appointments with homeowners to local contractors, billed per appointment that actually happens. Our first client agreed to this on a recorded call and saved his card through a $1 Stripe payment link, which we planned to use for billing later. That $1 payment went through. A few weeks later we invoiced him $1,500 for 3 completed appointments and charged the saved card. Stripe blocked the payment. Two days after that the account was closed with this wording: payments "don't appear to have been authorized by the customer." What happened next: - We appealed through the Dashboard with an appeal letter, our company documents and the invoice. It was rejected the next day as an "unacceptable level of risk." - Support told us our "business model presents a level of risk we're unable to support" and that the decision is final. - After a Stripe employee escalated it internally, we got a short email saying Stripe still won't accept payments for our business. In all of this, nobody asked us for the call recording, our messages with the client, or a confirmation from the client himself. As far as we know, he never disputed anything, and he has told us he is paying by bank transfer outside Stripe. I'm not saying our setup is perfect. It's a new account, the first real charge was large compared to the $1 test, and billing a saved card later is probably what looked wrong. If there's something specific we should fix, I'll fix it. What I'm asking: 1. Is there anyone at Stripe who can look at this with the evidence, including getting the client on a call? 2. For people who've been through this: how would you structure per-appointment billing so it doesn't look unauthorized (an invoice with a link each time, an email confirmation before each charge, something else)? I can share the account details, the call recording and the messages with anyone from Stripe who wants to look. Thanks for reading.

title: Piramida testów regresji
text: Dla przypomnienia, klasyczna piramida testów wygląda następująco i służy do wskazania ogólnych reguł prowadzenia testów: Uznane wśród testerów źródło roadmap.sh zdecydowało się opublikować swoją propozycję piramidy testów tylko dla testów regresji i możemy śmiało powiedzieć, że to dość osobliwa propozycja. Poniżej polska wersja: Nasza ocena 1. Jeśli akceptujemy, że piramida pokazuje również nakład pracy, to dolna warstwa z testami dymnymi powinna być najmniejsza. Wskazuje to więc, że piramida testów powinna być raczej wafelkiem (odwróconą piramidą), co symbolizuje najmniejszą liczbę testów dymnych i największą – pełnej regresji. 2. Warstwy w pierwotnej piramidzie miały przełożenie na poziomy testów i to miało sens. W tej piramidzie nie są to poziomy testów, a wszystko rozgrywa się w ramach jednej z metod prowadzenia testów. To powoduje, że można zaakceptować kolejność wykonania testów. Przeprowadzenie testów dymnych jest kryterium wstępnym – to się zgadza. Jednak zaraz po nich powinna zostać przeprowadzona ukierunkowana albo pełna regresja. Uruchomienie obu nie miałoby sensu. Autorzy tłumaczą, że ukierunkowana regresja koncentruje się na modyfikowanej funkcjonalności oraz powiązanych z nią ścieżkach w kodzie. Warstwa ta może obejmować testy jednostkowe, integracyjne oraz testy typu end-to-end, które sprawdzają zmienione obszary bez konieczności uruchamiania pełnego zestawu testów regresji. Jeśli jednak mamy dobrze przemyślaną regresję ukierunkowaną, po co uruchamiać jej pełną wersję? Stąd też nasza propozycja, aby to rozdzielić na dwie niezależne ścieżki. 3. Pierwotna piramida pokazuje, że testy z dolnej warstwy są najszybsze i najtańsze, gdy te na samej górze są najdroższe i najbardziej czasochłonne. To się w propozycji roadmap.sh akurat zgadza. Grafiki mają to do siebie, że powinny pomagać zrozumieć koncepcję, ale ponieważ ta konkretna odwołuje się do popularnego wzorca, wprowadza więcej zamieszania niż rozjaśnia. Gdy wchodzi się w polemikę ze standardem, potrzebny byłby szerszy opis tego, co autor miał na myśli. Oceniamy więc tę propozycję jako nie do końca trafioną i uważamy, że nie współgra ona z tym, co znamy z własnych projektów.

title: Software engineering after code becomes cheap with Satya Nadella
author: Gergely Orosz
text: Listen and watch now on YouTube , Apple , and Spotify . See the episode transcript at the top of this page, and timestamps for the episode at the bottom. Brought to You by • turbopuffer – a ridiculously scalable, fast and cheap hybrid search engine, built on top of object storage, used by cutting-edge companies like Anthropic, Linear, Ramp and many others. Many companies that switch to turbopuffer are cutting their search bills by 50% or more and getting much faster results. Check it out . Also, check out the new and improved The Pragmatic Engineer search I built on top of turbopuffer! • Linear – one of the big challenges for us devs is the sheer amount of code to review. Linear Diffs is a new feature for reviewing PRs inside of Linear, with all the context in one place. It also supports stacked PRs. Check it out • WorkOS – WorkOS built Airlock, the authorization layer for AI agents. It evaluates every request against the agent’s intent + your rules, and either allows it, denies it, or routes it to a human. Works with Claude Code, Codex & MCP gateways. Learn more In this episode What does software engineering look like when generating the code becomes cheap and verifying it is the hard part? There can be few people in tech more qualified to tackle this hot topic than Satya Nadella. Microsoft’s CEO started his career as a software engineer – a rare thing among Big Tech CEOs. Satya joins me to discuss how building software is changing at Microsoft, and what it means for us, software engineers. We start with Microsoft’s embrace of open source from the mid-2010s and the lessons learned from building VS Code in the open. I ask how Microsoft went from holding an early lead with GitHub Copilot to having to catch up with Cursor and Claude Code, and what it reveals about building products around rapidly improving models. Satya also explains what a “software factory” means to him, why specifications and verification are becoming more important, and how teams that work on products like the Windows operating system are adapting. We also touch on Microsoft’s voluntary exit offers, AI-related anxiety around engineering careers, and hear Nadella caution against drawing long-term conclusions from the slowdown in junior hiring. We also explore open and local models, why companies need to control their own AI infrastructure, and how to build safeguards around increasingly capable agents. Satya also has some advice for engineers who want to excel during this period of change – and why he would like to spend more time on building. Sidenote: we recorded this episode in Redmond just a few hours before Microsoft’s day-long Outlook outage, so there was no discussion of it. To the people asking : no, I did not pull out any cables during my visit that might have kicked out that outage :) However, I am already talking with the team inside Microsoft on-point for this outage, and expect a more detailed follow-up in the newsletter on what went wrong and what we can learn from it. Takeaways from the conversation with Satya I appreciated how grounded and thoughtful Satya was – and how pragmatic he is in suggesting to verify anything and everything related with LLMs, and not blindly trust anything or anyone (including vendors or AI models!) 12 of the most interesting takeaways I noted: 1. A new form of software engineering: teams building software factories to improve their work. Satya cites the Azure networking team which manages 500+ fiber network operators and recently built an agentic system to better manage emails and processes. Now, they operate much more efficiently as a result. Satya sees this as the reality of “AI transformation”: brownfield work on building software factories to improve how teams operate, all while continuing the day-to-day work. 2. GitHub Copilot fell behind Claude Code because the IDE faded out in just six months.
